editorial.hook: A farmhouse, a family at war over God, and a film that dares to mean it.
editorial.synopsis: A Danish farm in the 1920s. The old patriarch's faith is the stern Lutheran kind; his son has lost his; the neighbour's family belongs to a sect that treats them all as damned. In the middle of it walks another son, who went mad studying Kierkegaard and now believes he is Christ. Dreyer films it in long, slow, gliding takes, the camera drifting from face to face as if listening, the whitewashed rooms lit like paintings. For most of its length it is a family drama about doctrine. Then it asks you to believe something, and it does not blink. What happens in the last ten minutes is still argued about seventy years on.
editorial.whyItMatters: Winner of the Golden Lion at Venice in 1955 and the film Paul Schrader built his theory of transcendental style around; its unbroken takes and refusal of irony made it the ancestor of every film that treats faith as a formal problem rather than a theme.

editorial.hook: New York at night through a windshield, and the man behind it slowly coming apart.
editorial.synopsis: A Vietnam veteran who can't sleep takes a job driving a cab through the New York night, and the city pours in through his windshield: steam, neon, rain, bodies. He writes in a diary; he fixes on a campaign volunteer who is too clean for him and a child prostitute who isn't. Scorsese shoots the streets as if they were a fever and Bernard Herrmann's last score — a saxophone that keeps almost becoming a love theme — makes the loneliness nearly tender. You are inside this man's head whether you want to be or not. The film never tells you what to think of him. That is the problem it leaves you with.
editorial.whyItMatters: Palme d'Or 1976 and the definitive New Hollywood film: De Niro's Travis Bickle became the template for every alienated-man-in-the-city picture since, and the final sequence is still a case study in how editing and colour can make a scene feel like something the character is dreaming.

editorial.hook: Four people describe the same crime in a forest, and every one of them is lying.
editorial.synopsis: Rain hammers a ruined gate, and three men shelter under it, talking through a court case none of them can make sense of: a samurai is dead in a forest, his wife was attacked, a bandit has been caught. Then the film shows you the bandit's version, the wife's, the dead man's through a medium, and a witness's — and each one is a different film. Kurosawa shoots the forest as dazzle and shadow, the camera pointed straight into the sun through leaves, so that the light itself seems unreliable. By the end the question isn't what happened. It's whether anyone can tell the truth about themselves at all.
editorial.whyItMatters: The Golden Lion at Venice in 1951 announced Japanese cinema to the world and the film's structure gave a word to the language — 'the Rashomon effect' — for the idea that truth depends on who is telling it.

editorial.hook: A revolution filmed as if a newsreel crew had been there — and taking no side's comfort.
editorial.synopsis: Algiers, the late 1950s. In the Casbah, a petty criminal becomes a guerrilla; across the city, a French paratrooper colonel arrives to break the resistance by any method that works. Pontecorvo shot it on the actual streets with mostly non-professional actors, in grainy black and white that looks like news footage — it isn't, not a frame — and scores it to Ennio Morricone's drums and a single mournful theme. The bombs are placed by women in European dress. The torture is shown. The film understands both sides' logic completely and forgives neither. It moves like a thriller and lands like a history lesson you didn't want.
editorial.whyItMatters: Golden Lion 1966 and the founding film of Third Cinema's reach into Europe; banned in France for years, screened by the Black Panthers and the Pentagon alike, and still the clearest film ever made about how insurgency and counter-insurgency actually work.

editorial.hook: A director who can't make his film, so he makes this one out of the failure.
editorial.synopsis: A famous director arrives at a spa to recover and to finish the script for a huge science-fiction film he has no idea how to make. Producers hover, a mistress arrives, then a wife; a cardinal offers advice; a rocket launch tower stands half-built in a field. And between the demands, his mind slips — into childhood, into a harem of every woman he's known, into a dream of flying over a traffic jam. Fellini cuts between memory, fantasy and present without warning, and Nino Rota's circus music makes it all feel like a party you're slightly too tired for. It is a film about having nothing to say, and it says everything.
editorial.whyItMatters: Sixth in the 2022 directors' poll and the model for every film about making a film — Stardust Memories, All That Jazz, Synecdoche New York — because Fellini proved that the creative block itself could be the subject, and the form could be the mind in crisis.

editorial.hook: The hottest day of the year on one Brooklyn block, and everyone has a reason.
editorial.synopsis: One block in Bed-Stuy, one day, the heat already unbearable at breakfast. An Italian-American pizzeria, a Korean grocery, a corner of old men, a man with a boombox playing one song on repeat, a DJ in a window narrating the weather. Spike Lee shoots it in colours so saturated they seem to sweat — reds and oranges, Dutch angles, characters talking straight down the lens. Everyone is funny and everyone is right and everyone is a little bit wrong, and the film lets you feel that balance tipping degree by degree as the day goes on. It ends with two quotations, one from King and one from Malcolm X, and refuses to pick.
editorial.whyItMatters: Cahiers du Cinéma's film of the year in 1989 and the American film that most completely anticipated the next thirty years; its formal confidence — the stylisation, the direct address, the heat as structure — proved that a political film could also be a joyful one.

editorial.hook: Seven nights in Rome with a man who wanted to be a writer and became a guest.
editorial.synopsis: A gossip journalist drifts through Rome's night world — a film star wading into the Trevi Fountain, a fake miracle in a field, an intellectual's salon, an aristocrats' party in a castle, a dawn on a beach — never quite joining any of it and never quite leaving. Fellini builds the film in episodes rather than a plot, each one a long night that ends in grey morning light, and Marcello Mastroianni wears the same beautiful suit through all of them with the expression of a man waiting for his life to start. The word 'paparazzo' comes from this film. So does a certain idea of Rome that the city has been living up to ever since.
editorial.whyItMatters: Palme d'Or 1960 and the film that broke Fellini out of neorealism into something no one had a name for yet: the episodic, the autobiographical, the modern — a portrait of a culture with everything except a reason, which turned out to describe the next sixty years.

editorial.hook: The life of a donkey, from owner to owner, and the whole of human cruelty passing through.
editorial.synopsis: A donkey is born on a farm in rural France, is named by children, and is passed from hand to hand for the rest of his life — a baker, a drunk, a miller, a circus, a gang of boys — while a girl who loved him as a child grows up alongside and is passed around just as carelessly. Bresson uses non-actors and asks them to do nothing, and he films the donkey's eyes the way other directors film a star. There is almost no music except a Schubert sonata that returns like a memory. Nothing is explained or underlined. By the end, an animal that cannot speak has become the only character you fully understand.
editorial.whyItMatters: Cahiers' film of the year in 1966 and the purest statement of Bresson's method — performance stripped to gesture, meaning built from cuts — which Godard called 'the world in an hour and a half' and which taught Haneke, the Dardennes and Reichardt how to make feeling out of restraint.

editorial.hook: A dying man's last word, and a film that fails — beautifully — to explain it.
editorial.synopsis: A newspaper tycoon dies in a palace full of things he never unpacked, and his last word is a puzzle. A reporter sets out to solve it by interviewing everyone who knew him, and each interview is a different account of a different Kane: the idealist, the demagogue, the husband, the tyrant. Welles was twenty-five and had never made a film, so he did everything the manual said not to — deep focus where the whole room is sharp, ceilings in shot, overlapping dialogue, a story told in loops. The film is nimble and funny and sad, and it ends with an answer that explains nothing, which is the point.
editorial.whyItMatters: First on TSPDT's aggregated list and the top of the Sight & Sound critics' poll for fifty years; nearly every technique of modern film grammar is either introduced or perfected here, and the structure — a life assembled from witnesses who contradict each other — is still the template for the biographical film.

editorial.hook: Two families, one house, and a staircase the whole film is built around.
editorial.synopsis: A family of four lives in a semi-basement in Seoul, folding pizza boxes for cash and leaning out the window to catch a neighbour's wifi. Then the son gets a job tutoring a rich family's daughter in a hillside house made of glass and concrete, and one by one, with forged credentials and perfect timing, the rest of his family finds their way in. Bong Joon-ho directs it as a comedy of manners that keeps changing genre underneath you, and the house itself — stairs, windows, a garden lit like a stage — becomes the film's argument about who gets to stand above whom. You laugh for an hour. Then it rains.
editorial.whyItMatters: Palme d'Or 2019, then the first film not in English to win Best Picture, and the moment Korean cinema's two-decade rise became undeniable; its precision about class — told entirely through architecture and movement — made it the rare film to be both a global phenomenon and a formal object worth studying.

editorial.hook: From a thrown bone to the end of the universe, almost without words.
editorial.synopsis: Apes on a plain discover a black slab and then a weapon. Four million years later, a spacecraft waltzes toward a space station to Strauss, and a scientist flies to the Moon to look at another slab. Then a mission to Jupiter, two astronauts, and a computer with a soft voice that is the only character in the film with feelings. Kubrick cuts out nearly all the talking and lets images and music do what exposition would ruin — the match cut across millions of years, the silence of space, the light show that may be a birth. It is slow, cold and enormous, and the longer you look the less it explains and the more it seems to know.
editorial.whyItMatters: Voted the greatest film ever made in the 2022 Sight & Sound directors' poll; Kubrick proved a film could be philosophy without words, and every ambitious science-fiction picture since — Solaris, Blade Runner, Arrival — has been in conversation with it.

title: Jeanne Dielman, 23, quai du Commerce, 1080 Bruxelles

editorial.hook: Three days of housework in real time. On the second day, something is off.
editorial.synopsis: A widow in a Brussels flat does the same things in the same order: makes coffee, peels potatoes, bathes, shines her son's shoes, receives a male visitor in the afternoon to pay the bills, cooks dinner. Akerman shows it at the length it takes, from a camera that sits at her own eye level and never moves, for over three hours. You learn the kitchen. You learn the rhythm. And on the second day you start noticing that a lid is left off, a button is missed, the potatoes are overcooked — and the dread that builds from those details is unlike anything in a thriller, because the film has taught you exactly how much they matter.
editorial.whyItMatters: Voted the greatest film of all time in the 2022 Sight & Sound critics' poll — the first film by a woman to top it — and the film that made duration itself a subject; every slow-cinema director since has been working in the room Akerman built.

editorial.hook: A river journey into Vietnam that becomes a journey into the people who sent him.
editorial.synopsis: A captain in Saigon is given a mission he isn't supposed to talk about: travel upriver into Cambodia and kill a decorated colonel who has gone off the map and started his own war. The boat trip is the film, and every stop on it is a different kind of madness — a surf-obsessed cavalry officer, a USO show that turns into a riot, a bridge that is rebuilt every night and destroyed every morning. Coppola nearly lost his mind and his money making it, and it shows in the best way: the film has the scale of a nightmare, the Doors on the soundtrack, and a final hour that drifts into fog and ritual and refuses to come back out.
editorial.whyItMatters: Palme d'Or 1979 and the last great monument of New Hollywood's ambition before the blockbuster era closed the door; Conrad's Heart of Darkness transposed to a war America was still trying not to think about, and a production so legendary it became its own documentary.

editorial.hook: An old man drives to collect a prize, and his whole life gets in the car.
editorial.synopsis: A distinguished, chilly old professor sets off by car to receive an honorary degree, with his daughter-in-law — who does not much like him — along for the ride. On the way he picks up hitchhikers, stops at the house where he spent childhood summers, and starts to dream: a street with clocks without hands, a coffin that spills his own body, an exam he cannot pass. Bergman cast Victor Sjöström, the great silent-era director, in the lead, and his face does the film's work — a man realising, too late and in time, what he withheld from the people around him. It is warm in a way Bergman rarely allowed himself, and the warmth is earned.
editorial.whyItMatters: Golden Bear at Berlin in 1958 and the film that made Bergman's name outside Sweden; its structure — a day's journey braided with dreams and memory — became a model for how cinema could show a mind reckoning with itself, and Woody Allen spent a career trying to remake it.

editorial.hook: A woman who chose silence arrives with a daughter, a piano and a will of iron.
editorial.synopsis: A mute Scotswoman is sold into marriage to a settler in colonial New Zealand and lands on a grey beach with her young daughter and her piano. The husband leaves the piano on the sand. A neighbour who has gone half-native buys it, and offers to let her earn it back one key at a time, one visit at a time. Campion films the bush as mud and rain and tangled green, and Holly Hunter plays the whole film with her face and her hands — the piano is her voice, literally, and when she plays, the film goes quiet to listen. It is a Gothic romance, a colonial critique and a study of desire that owes nobody an apology.
editorial.whyItMatters: Palme d'Or 1993, shared, making Campion the first woman to win it, and the film that showed a period romance could be made entirely from a woman's point of view and lose none of its heat; Hunter and Anna Paquin both won Oscars for playing people who barely speak.

editorial.hook: A Paris of glass and steel where nothing goes wrong and everything goes slightly wrong.
editorial.synopsis: Monsieur Hulot — raincoat, pipe, umbrella — wanders into a modern Paris that Tati built from scratch on a vast lot outside the city: glass office blocks, a trade fair, an airport, a restaurant opening the night before it's finished. There is barely a plot and barely a close-up. Instead the frame fills with dozens of people doing dozens of small things at once, and you choose where to look — a door that makes no sound, a chair that sighs, tourists photographing a reflection of the Eiffel Tower in a glass door because the real one is out of frame. The restaurant sequence, nearly an hour long, slowly falls apart into the happiest chaos ever filmed.
editorial.whyItMatters: Tati bankrupted himself building 'Tativille' for it and the film sank on release; now it sits at 23 in the Sight & Sound critics' poll as the most generous comedy ever made — a film that trusts its audience to find the jokes, and has a different one for every seat in the house.

editorial.hook: A Paris boy nobody wants, running — and a final frame that stops him and looks at you.
editorial.synopsis: A twelve-year-old in Paris is in trouble at school, in the way at home, and most alive on the streets with his one friend — skipping class for the cinema, stealing a typewriter, lying with a straight face. His parents are not monsters, which is worse; they just don't have room for him. Truffaut shot it on real streets with a boy, Jean-Pierre Léaud, who seems to be inventing himself in front of the camera, and the film has a freedom in its movement that was new: a long tracking shot of children running, a spinning fairground ride, an interview with a psychologist where Léaud simply talks. The last shot is a freeze frame on a beach, and cinema had not ended a film like that before.
editorial.whyItMatters: The film that opened the French New Wave at Cannes in 1959 — Truffaut was 27, had been banned from the festival the year before as a critic, and won Best Director; Léaud's Antoine Doinel would return in four more films across twenty years, the first time cinema followed a character through a whole life.

editorial.hook: A marriage ends during a film shoot in Capri, in widescreen and primary colours.
editorial.synopsis: A screenwriter takes a job rewriting a film of The Odyssey for a vulgar American producer and a tired German director — played by Fritz Lang, as himself. His wife comes along. Somewhere in a half-hour scene in their Rome apartment, in which they talk and bathe and argue and pass each other in doorways, she stops loving him, and neither of them can say exactly when. Godard films it in widescreen reds and blues against the Mediterranean, with a Georges Delerue theme so grave and lovely it feels like a funeral for the whole idea of romance. It is his most beautiful film and his saddest, and the two things are the same thing.
editorial.whyItMatters: Cahiers' film of the year in 1963 and the Godard that even people who dislike Godard surrender to; a film about the death of classical cinema made in its most classical form, with Brigitte Bardot and Fritz Lang standing in for everything Hollywood and Europe had been to each other.

editorial.hook: A life remembered out of order: a mother, a burning barn, wind in a field.
editorial.synopsis: A dying man remembers, and the film is the remembering: a woman sitting on a fence waiting for a husband who won't come, a barn burning in the rain while a family watches, a printing-house panic over a possible typo, newsreels of the Spanish Civil War and the Soviet army crossing a lake. His mother and his wife are played by the same actress; the boy he was and the son he has are the same boy. Tarkovsky's own father reads his poems on the soundtrack. There is no plot to follow and no need to — the film moves like memory does, by association and weather, and it may be the closest cinema has come to showing what it is like to be inside a mind.
editorial.whyItMatters: Eighth in the 2022 directors' poll and Tarkovsky's most personal film; Soviet authorities called it incomprehensible and buried it, and it has since become the model for every film that tries to make memory itself the structure, from Malick's The Tree of Life to Aftersun.

editorial.hook: A woman disappears on an island, and the film forgets to look for her — on purpose.
editorial.synopsis: A party of wealthy Romans sails to a volcanic island off Sicily. One of the women wanders off and is never seen again. Her lover and her best friend search, then keep searching on the mainland, then slowly, without quite deciding to, become a couple themselves. Antonioni was booed at Cannes for this: a mystery that abandons its mystery, characters who drift through empty towns and grand hotels looking at nothing, shots held long after the people have left the frame. Monica Vitti's face is the film's landscape, and the actual landscape — rock, sea, baroque facades, a deserted new town — is as expressive as any face. Nothing happens, exactly. Everything is felt.
editorial.whyItMatters: Second on the Sight & Sound critics' list within two years of its release and the film that invented a cinema of alienation — where the architecture is the drama and the plot is what the characters are avoiding; Antonioni's trilogy with Vitti begins here.

editorial.hook: A village hires seven men, and three hours later you know every one of them.
editorial.synopsis: Bandits will come when the barley is ripe, so a farming village sends its men to the town to find samurai who will fight for food. They find a weary veteran, who finds the others — a young disciple, an old friend, an archer, a cheerful fencer, a master swordsman who wants only to perfect himself, and a wild farmer's son pretending to be a samurai. Kurosawa takes an hour just to gather them and makes every minute count, so that by the time the rain-soaked final battle arrives you are not watching action, you are watching people you know try not to die. Toshiro Mifune's performance as the imposter is one of the great physical performances in cinema.
editorial.whyItMatters: Number 10 on TSPDT's aggregated list and the most influential action film ever made — remade as The Magnificent Seven, borrowed by Star Wars, Pixar and a thousand ensemble films — but what it actually taught was patience: that a battle means nothing until you have lived with the people fighting it.

editorial.hook: A detective afraid of heights follows a woman and falls a different way.
editorial.synopsis: A San Francisco detective, retired after a rooftop fall left him with vertigo and a dead colleague, takes a private job following an old friend's wife, who seems possessed by a woman dead a hundred years. He follows her through a museum, a florist, a cemetery, a mission bell tower, and his watching becomes something else. Hitchcock films the city in greens and reds, dresses Kim Novak in grey, and makes the camera itself dizzy — the shot that zooms in while tracking out was invented for this. The second half, which no one who hasn't seen it should know anything about, turns a thriller into the most naked film ever made about wanting a person to be someone they are not.
editorial.whyItMatters: Topped the Sight & Sound critics' poll in 2012 and sits second in 2022, after half a century as a commercial failure and a critical afterthought; the film that made the case for Hitchcock as an artist and for the idea that a thriller could be a confession.

editorial.hook: A young woman found frozen in a ditch, and the people who watched her pass.
editorial.synopsis: The film opens on a body in a vineyard ditch in winter, a young woman nobody knows. Then it goes back: a few weeks of her drifting through the south of France with a tent and a rucksack, hitching rides, sleeping in barns, taking work and leaving it, being helped and used and ignored. Varda structures it as a kind of inquest — the people who met her speak to the camera as if being interviewed — but refuses to explain her. Sandrine Bonnaire plays her as neither victim nor rebel, just someone who said no to everything and kept walking. The camera tracks right to left, against the grain, every time she moves on. It is cold, unsentimental and quietly furious.
editorial.whyItMatters: Golden Lion 1985 and Varda's most complete film: a portrait of freedom as refusal, made with a documentary's structure and a fiction's compassion, and the clearest demonstration of why she was the New Wave's conscience as well as its mother.

editorial.hook: An Irish rogue climbs into the aristocracy, in paintings that happen to move.
editorial.synopsis: A young Irishman of no fortune falls in love, fights a duel, flees, is robbed, joins the British army, deserts, joins the Prussian army, becomes a spy, a gambler, and finally the husband of one of the richest women in England — and that is only the first half. Kubrick shot it in candlelight with lenses built for NASA, composed every frame like a Gainsborough, and set it to Handel and Schubert played at the pace of a funeral march. A narrator tells you what will happen before it does. The effect is of watching a life from a great height, and the slow zoom-out that opens nearly every scene — from a face to a landscape — is the film's whole philosophy in a gesture.
editorial.whyItMatters: Dismissed as a cold museum piece in 1975 and now 12th in the Sight & Sound directors' poll; the most beautiful film ever shot by most measures, and the one that proved Kubrick's detachment was a form of pity — the camera keeps pulling back because it cannot bear to stay close.

editorial.hook: A prisoner, a cell, a spoon, and the most suspenseful patience in cinema.
editorial.synopsis: Lyon, 1943. A Resistance fighter is in a Gestapo prison awaiting execution, and he intends to leave. Bresson shows you how, step by step: a spoon sharpened on the floor into a chisel, boards loosened a millimetre a day, wire from a bed frame braided into rope, lantern frames bent into hooks. The camera stays on hands and objects; the sound — footsteps, keys, a distant tram — is the whole outside world. The title tells you the ending and it changes nothing, because the suspense isn't whether but how, and whether the young cellmate who arrives at the end is a gift or a trap. The Kyrie from Mozart's Mass in C minor plays over slop buckets. Grace, Bresson says, looks like this.
editorial.whyItMatters: Cahiers' film of the year in 1956 and Best Director at Cannes 1957; the proof that Bresson's austerity could produce more tension than any thriller, and a film whose attention to process — hands, tools, time — echoes through Melville, Michael Mann and the Dardennes.

editorial.hook: A man, his son, and one day in Rome searching for the bicycle his job depends on.
editorial.synopsis: Postwar Rome. A man who has been out of work for two years gets a job pasting up posters — but only if he has a bicycle. His wife pawns the bedsheets to get his out of hock. On his first morning it is stolen. The rest of the film is one day: the man and his small son walking the city, through markets and churches and a brothel and a fortune-teller's flat, looking for one bicycle among thousands. De Sica cast a factory worker and a boy he found in the street, shot on real locations with real crowds, and the result is so direct it feels less like a film than like something you witnessed. The boy's face, watching his father, is where the film lives.
editorial.whyItMatters: The defining film of Italian Neorealism and number 15 on TSPDT's list; it taught the world — Ray in India, the Iranian New Wave, the Dardennes — that a camera on an ordinary street, pointed at an ordinary crisis, could be the whole of cinema.

editorial.hook: A boy, his sister, and a Bengali village seen so closely you can hear the rain coming.
editorial.synopsis: A poor Brahmin family in a Bengal village: a father who dreams of being a writer, a mother holding everything together with nothing, a daughter who steals fruit from the neighbour's orchard, an ancient aunt, and a small boy named Apu, watching all of it. Ray shot it over three years, whenever he could borrow money, with a crew that had never made a film, and it shows nothing that a plot would need — a train glimpsed through tall grass, a sweet-seller followed by children and a dog, a monsoon arriving on a pond's surface, the aunt's water pot rolling away. Ravi Shankar's sitar carries it. It is the most tender first film ever made, and the most unsentimental about what poverty costs.
editorial.whyItMatters: Number 35 in the 2022 Sight & Sound critics' poll and the film that founded Indian Parallel Cinema; Ray saw Bicycle Thieves in London and went home to make this, and the trilogy it opens — following Apu to manhood — is cinema's great account of a life.

title: The Passion of Joan of Arc

editorial.hook: A trial told almost entirely in faces, and one face never matched since.
editorial.synopsis: Joan of Arc's trial for heresy, taken from the actual transcripts, and filmed almost entirely in close-up — the judges' faces looming and warted and sneering, and in the middle, Renée Falconetti, in her only film role, with no make-up, her head shaved on camera, tears standing in her eyes for what seems like the entire running time. Dreyer built full sets and then barely showed them; the camera tilts and swoops at strange angles, the cuts come fast, and the effect is of being trapped inside an interrogation. The original negative was lost in a fire and the film survived for decades in compromised versions, until a complete print turned up in a Norwegian mental hospital in 1981.
editorial.whyItMatters: Number 19 on TSPDT's list and the summit of silent cinema's last year; Falconetti's performance is the one every account of screen acting eventually returns to, and Dreyer's refusal of the long shot — the whole film as a face — had no precedent and still has no equal.

editorial.hook: A country-house weekend where everyone loves the wrong person and dances anyway.
editorial.synopsis: An aviator lands after a record flight and announces on the radio that the woman he did it for didn't come to meet him. The woman is married to a marquis who has a mistress; the marquis invites them all to his château for a hunting weekend, along with a crowd of friends, and below stairs the servants are running the same comedy with different accents. Renoir plays the hapless go-between himself. The camera moves through the house in long takes with half a dozen things happening at every depth, and a hunt where rabbits and pheasants are shot in a long, cold montage tells you what the party is really about. It is light as champagne and it ends in a death everyone agrees to call an accident.
editorial.whyItMatters: Booed, cut, banned by Vichy and the Nazis, lost in a bombing and reassembled from fragments; now fifth on TSPDT's aggregated list and the film that taught the deep-focus long take to Welles and the ensemble comedy of manners to Altman — a portrait of a society a few months before it collapsed.

editorial.hook: A novice visits her uncle before her vows. Buñuel makes sure she never returns.
editorial.synopsis: A young woman about to become a nun is sent to visit her widowed uncle, who notices she looks exactly like his dead wife. After that, nothing goes as anyone intends. She inherits his estate, fills it with beggars and cripples as an act of charity, and the beggars, left alone one night, stage a banquet that arranges itself — for one frozen second — into Leonardo's Last Supper, scored to Handel's Messiah. Buñuel had been invited back to Franco's Spain to make a film after twenty-five years in exile; this is what he made. It is calm, elegant, deadpan, and about as blasphemous as cinema has ever been while keeping a straight face.
editorial.whyItMatters: Palme d'Or 1961, then immediately banned in Spain and denounced by the Vatican; the film that marked Buñuel's return to Europe and his late masterwork period, and the finest example of his method — surrealism not as spectacle but as a logic that lets the world indict itself.

editorial.hook: A car thief, an American girl, and a camera that cuts whenever it feels like it.
editorial.synopsis: A small-time crook steals a car in Marseille, shoots a policeman on the road to Paris, and spends the rest of the film hiding out with an American student who sells the Herald Tribune on the Champs-Élysées, trying to collect a debt and persuade her to run away with him. Belmondo rubs his lip like Bogart; Jean Seberg's cropped hair became a decade's haircut. Godard shot it handheld on the streets, pushed the cameraman around in a wheelchair, and when the film ran too long, cut inside the shots instead of between them — the jump cut, which looked like a mistake and turned out to be a new grammar. It feels like it was made this morning.
editorial.whyItMatters: The French New Wave's manifesto film and 38th in the 2022 critics' poll; nearly every rule of continuity editing is broken on purpose here, and the sense that cinema could be made quickly, cheaply and personally by someone who loved movies — not by a studio — begins with it.

editorial.hook: A preacher with LOVE and HATE on his knuckles, in a fairy tale shot as a nightmare.
editorial.synopsis: A self-ordained preacher with a switchblade and 'LOVE' and 'HATE' tattooed on his fingers shares a cell with a condemned man who hid stolen money somewhere his children know about. Released, the preacher heads for the widow and the children. Charles Laughton — a great actor directing his only film — shot it as a child's dream of the Depression: a river journey past giant frogs and owls, a house like a paper cut-out, Robert Mitchum's shadow on a bedroom wall singing a hymn. The second half belongs to Lillian Gish, a shotgun across her lap on a porch, singing back. It is terrifying and tender in equal measure and looks like nothing else made in Hollywood.
editorial.whyItMatters: A flop so complete that Laughton never directed again; now 25th in the Sight & Sound critics' poll, and the film in which German Expressionism, Southern Gothic and silent-era lyricism meet — a lineage that runs forward to Lynch, the Coens and every film that treats childhood as a horror story.

editorial.hook: Three and a half hours of a man talking, and the women who stop listening.
editorial.synopsis: A young man in Paris after 1968 lives with an older woman who supports him, picks up a nurse in a café, and spends the film talking — to both of them, about both of them, about Proust and the Resistance and his own magnificence — in cafés, beds and borrowed rooms. Eustache shot it in grainy black and white with almost no camera movement and scenes that run as long as the conversations, and Jean-Pierre Léaud, the New Wave's eternal boy, plays the talker as someone whose charm has curdled into a way of not feeling anything. Then, in the last half hour, the nurse speaks, and the film turns on its axis. It is the funeral of a generation's idea of itself.
editorial.whyItMatters: Grand Prix at Cannes 1973 and the film that closed the French New Wave — Eustache made it as an epitaph and killed himself eight years later; its marathon talk, its cruelty to its own hero and its final monologue reshaped what a film about love was allowed to be.

editorial.hook: A medieval icon painter who stops painting, across a Russia of mud, invasion and a bell.
editorial.synopsis: Fifteenth-century Russia in eight chapters: a man flies in a balloon and crashes; a jester is arrested; monks argue about faith in the rain; Tatars sack a cathedral; a painter who has seen too much takes a vow of silence and gives up his art. The painter is Andrei Rublev, Russia's greatest icon maker, and the film is not his biography but his world — three hours of mud, horses, snow, smoke and faces, shot in black and white so deep it feels carved. Then, in the final chapter, a boy who claims to know his dead father's secret is ordered to cast a great bell, and Tarkovsky films the whole process, pit to first ring, as the most moving account of making something that exists.
editorial.whyItMatters: Banned at home for five years, smuggled to Cannes in 1969 and 28th on TSPDT's list; the film that established Tarkovsky as the heir to Dostoevsky — a historical epic that is really an argument about whether art is possible in a cruel world, answered in colour in the last five minutes.

editorial.hook: A wedding in the sun, a study in shadow, and a son who swore he wasn't like his family.
editorial.synopsis: A Mafia don holds court in his darkened study on the day of his daughter's wedding, granting favours while the party blazes in the garden outside. His youngest son, a war hero in uniform, tells his girlfriend that's his family, not him. The film is the slow, patient proof that he's wrong. Coppola shot it in browns and golds and blacks, Gordon Willis letting faces fall into shadow until you lean forward to find them, and Nino Rota's waltz plays over everything like a memory of the old country. It is operatic and intimate at once, and the famous set pieces — the horse, the restaurant, the baptism — matter less than the quiet in Al Pacino's face as it closes.
editorial.whyItMatters: Third in the 2022 Sight & Sound directors' poll and the film that made New Hollywood's revolution commercial: a studio picture with the texture and moral seriousness of European art cinema, which taught a generation that darkness — literal and otherwise — could be popular.

editorial.hook: Newlyweds on a canal barge — the most romantic film ever made about boredom.
editorial.synopsis: A village girl marries a barge captain and walks straight from the church to the boat, in her wedding dress, to begin a life on the canals between Le Havre and Paris. Aboard are a cabin boy, a dozen cats, and an old mate — Michel Simon, extraordinary — with a cabin full of junk from around the world and a jar containing his dead friend's hands. She is restless; Paris glitters in the distance; a peddler flirts. Vigo, dying of tuberculosis at 29, shot it in winter fog and filmed a sequence of the husband diving into the canal to find his wife's face in the water that is as close to pure longing as cinema gets. The studio recut it. He never saw the restored version.
editorial.whyItMatters: Vigo's only feature and 21st on TSPDT's list; a film that takes poetic realism's working-class settings and floods them with surrealist tenderness, and a direct ancestor of Truffaut, Carax and anyone who has filmed water as if it were feeling.

editorial.hook: One night in Milan at the end of a marriage, at a party nobody wants to be at.
editorial.synopsis: A novelist and his wife visit a dying friend in a hospital, attend his book launch, and go to an all-night party at an industrialist's villa, and somewhere across those eighteen hours they realise they no longer love each other. Antonioni follows Jeanne Moreau on a long walk through Milan's new suburbs — glass towers, wasteland, a rocket launched by boys in a field — and the city's modernity becomes the marriage's emptiness made visible. Mastroianni drifts; Monica Vitti arrives at the party as a temptation neither is sure they want. The final scene, at dawn on a golf course, with a letter read aloud, is one of the most devastating in all cinema and nothing in it is raised above a murmur.
editorial.whyItMatters: Golden Bear at Berlin in 1961 and the centre of Antonioni's trilogy about modern alienation; the film where his use of architecture as emotion reached its purest form, and the template for every film in which a long night at a party ends a relationship.

editorial.hook: Ninety minutes of a singer's afternoon in Paris, waiting to hear whether she is dying.
editorial.synopsis: A pop singer in Paris has had a test for cancer and will get the results at seven. The film is what she does with the two hours before: a tarot reading, a taxi, a hat shop, a rehearsal with her songwriters, a walk through Montparnasse, a park, a soldier on leave from Algeria who talks to her as no one else has. Varda shot it in close to real time, with the hour marked in chapter titles, and the city — mirrors, shop windows, street performers, a frog-swallower — keeps reflecting her back at herself. The film pivots on a single song, performed straight to camera, after which she takes off her wig and starts, for the first time, to look outward.
editorial.whyItMatters: Fourteenth in the 2022 Sight & Sound critics' poll and the French New Wave's great film about being looked at; Varda turned a woman's fear into a structure and a city into a mirror, and made the first feminist film of the movement without a word of doctrine.

editorial.hook: A tramp, a blind flower girl, and the greatest final close-up in cinema.
editorial.synopsis: The Tramp meets a blind flower seller who mistakes him for a millionaire, and he spends the film trying to stay that millionaire for her — boxing for prize money, sweeping streets, befriending an actual millionaire who only recognises him when drunk. Chaplin made it three years after sound arrived and refused to speak, shooting the flower-girl meeting over a year and more than three hundred takes until it was right. The comedy is as precise as a watch — the boxing match is one of the funniest sequences ever filmed — and it exists to earn the ending, in which a woman who can now see looks at the man in front of her and the film cuts to his face. That cut is the whole art.
editorial.whyItMatters: Number 26 on TSPDT's list and Chaplin's own favourite of his films; the summit of silent comedy made in defiance of sound, and the proof — in its final shot, which Orson Welles called the greatest in cinema — that a face can hold more than any line.

editorial.hook: A time-travel story told in still photographs — and one single second of movement.
editorial.synopsis: After a third world war, survivors in the tunnels under Paris experiment on prisoners, sending their minds into the past in search of help. The subject is a man haunted by one childhood memory: a woman's face on the observation pier at Orly airport, and a man dying. The whole film is black-and-white still photographs, dissolving one into the next, with a narrator and a whispered German soundtrack — and then, for a moment, a woman asleep in bed opens her eyes and the image moves. Twenty-eight minutes long, Marker's film about memory, love and the impossibility of escaping your own past has the weight of an epic. The ending closes a loop you have been inside since the first frame.
editorial.whyItMatters: Thirty-fifth in the 2022 directors' poll despite being under half an hour; the most influential short film ever made — remade as 12 Monkeys, echoed in everything from Terminator to Arrival — and the proof that cinema is made of time, not motion.

editorial.hook: A wife who loves too loudly, and a camera that will not look away.
editorial.synopsis: A Los Angeles housewife, married to a construction foreman, loves her husband and her three children with an intensity that keeps spilling over the edges of what is allowed — she talks too much, touches too much, makes faces, asks strangers in for spaghetti at six in the morning. He loves her back and has no idea what to do. Cassavetes shot it in his own house with his wife, Gena Rowlands, and his friend Peter Falk, in long handheld takes that let scenes go on past the point where other films would cut, and the result is less a story than a pressure chamber. Rowlands' performance is one of the two or three greatest ever filmed. The question of who is actually unwell is never settled.
editorial.whyItMatters: Eighteenth in the 2022 directors' poll and the film that made Cassavetes' method undeniable: independent, self-financed, actor-first, and so raw that American cinema has been chasing its honesty ever since, from Scorsese to the Safdies.

editorial.hook: Two partisans cross a frozen Belarus, and the film becomes a passion play.
editorial.synopsis: Belarus, 1942, deep winter. Two Soviet partisans leave their starving unit to find food in a village and are captured by the Germans and their collaborators. One is a soldier who has always been brave; the other is a quiet schoolteacher who has never had to find out. Shepitko films the snow as a white that burns, the faces in close-ups that owe everything to Dreyer, and the interrogation and its aftermath as a slow moral exchange between the two men — one coming apart, one, against all reason, becoming calm. The religious shape of the story is impossible to miss and the film never says the word. It is the greatest Soviet war film and one of the great films about faith.
editorial.whyItMatters: Golden Bear at Berlin in 1977 and Larisa Shepitko's last film — she died in a car crash two years later at 41; her husband Elem Klimov's Come and See is its companion and successor, and the two together are the summit of Soviet cinema's reckoning with the war.

editorial.hook: A daughter who will not leave her widowed father, and a father who lies to make her go.
editorial.synopsis: A grown daughter keeps house for her widowed father in postwar Kamakura, and she is content; everyone around her — an aunt, a friend, the father himself — decides she must marry. She refuses, laughing, then not laughing. The father, who wants nothing but her company, begins to pretend he plans to remarry so that she will feel free. Ozu films it at tatami height in his still, square frames: a bicycle ride by the sea, a Noh performance where the daughter's face slowly changes as she watches her father watch another woman, a last trip to Kyoto, a vase in a dark room. The final scene — a man alone, peeling an apple — is the most quietly shattering ending in cinema.
editorial.whyItMatters: Twenty-first in the 2022 Sight & Sound critics' poll and the first of Ozu's great late films with Setsuko Hara; the model for his entire mature style — the low camera, the pillow shots, the family as the only subject — and the one in which the cost of love is counted most exactly.

editorial.hook: He says they met here last year. She says they didn't. The film agrees with both.
editorial.synopsis: In a baroque hotel of endless corridors, mirrors and formal gardens where the people cast shadows but the trees don't, a man approaches a woman and tells her they met last year, here or somewhere like here, and that she promised to leave with him. She doesn't remember. He describes it again. The film shows it, or shows something — the same scene in different rooms, different dresses, the same words in a different order — while a narrator murmurs and an organ plays. Resnais and the novelist Alain Robbe-Grillet built a film with no reliable past and no present tense, and it is either the most beautiful puzzle in cinema or a dream you are having about one.
editorial.whyItMatters: Golden Lion 1961 and the film that pushed cinema's relationship with memory and time to its furthest point; endlessly parodied, endlessly imitated — Kubrick's Overlook corridors, Lynch's doubled women, Nolan's unreliable chronologies all begin in this hotel.

editorial.hook: A Sicilian prince watches his world end at a ball that lasts forty-five minutes.
editorial.synopsis: Sicily, 1860. Garibaldi's redshirts are landing, the old aristocracy is finished, and a prince — Burt Lancaster, dubbed into Italian and never better — understands it before anyone else: 'everything must change so that everything can stay the same.' His nephew joins the revolution and marries the beautiful daughter of a vulgar new-money mayor, and the prince arranges it all with a tired grace. Visconti, a Marxist aristocrat himself, films it in the actual palaces with the actual furniture, and ends with a ball that runs nearly an hour — waltzes, sweat, a prince alone in a room full of chamber pots looking at a painting of a deathbed — which is the whole film's meaning in motion.
editorial.whyItMatters: Palme d'Or 1963 and the greatest historical film ever made by most accounts; Visconti's elegy for his own class, which Coppola studied for The Godfather and Scorsese for The Age of Innocence, and whose ball sequence is cinema's definitive image of a world ending in public.

editorial.hook: A brother and sister, both wrecks, under one roof — Cassavetes' last word on love.
editorial.synopsis: A novelist who researches love by filling his house with call girls and a woman whose divorce has left her with nothing to pour herself into are brother and sister, and she turns up on his doorstep with a taxi full of luggage and, later, a goat, two miniature horses and a duck. Cassavetes plays him, dying as he shot it; Gena Rowlands plays her as someone whose love is so total it has nowhere to land. The film drifts between their two disasters, breaks into an opera dream sequence, and settles into a long rainy night in which two people who cannot be fixed take care of each other anyway. 'Love is a stream,' she says. 'It's continuous. It doesn't stop.'
editorial.whyItMatters: Golden Bear at Berlin in 1984 and Cassavetes' farewell; the most tender of his films and the summary of everything he believed — that feeling is the only subject, that performance is a form of truth, and that a film can be as untidy as a life and still be shaped.

editorial.hook: A boxer who can take any punch except the ones he throws at the people who love him.
editorial.synopsis: Jake LaMotta, middleweight, fights his way through the 1940s and 1950s — in the ring, in his kitchen, in his own head. He is jealous of his wife to the point of madness, suspicious of his brother who manages him, and only ever at peace when someone is hitting him. Scorsese shot the fights in black and white as if they were happening inside a migraine — flashbulbs, blood spraying in slow motion, the ring expanding and shrinking from shot to shot — and De Niro gained sixty pounds to play the bloated, washed-up LaMotta reciting Brando to a dressing-room mirror. It is not a sports film. It is a film about a man who cannot be loved because he cannot stop punishing himself.
editorial.whyItMatters: Twenty-second in the 2022 directors' poll and the film Scorsese made when he thought he was finished; a masterwork of editing — Thelma Schoonmaker won her first Oscar for it — and the moment American cinema's great director found his permanent subject, the violence men do to themselves.

editorial.hook: Taipei, 1960: teenage gangs, Elvis records, and a nation in exile from itself.
editorial.synopsis: Taipei, 1960. A fourteen-year-old boy from a mainlander family — his parents fled China with the Nationalists and are still waiting to go back — drifts between night school, a street gang, a girl with a dangerous ex-boyfriend, and a radio that plays Elvis. Edward Yang built the film from a real murder case and shot it over four hours with a cast of mostly first-time teenagers, in long wide shots where the camera stays back and lets you find the drama in a doorway or a flashlight beam. It is about adolescence and gangs the way The Godfather is about business: the real subject is a whole society in exile, improvising a culture from American records and Japanese houses.
editorial.whyItMatters: The peak of New Taiwanese Cinema alongside Yi Yi and 78th in the 2022 critics' poll; nearly impossible to see for twenty years, it emerged in restoration as the most complete portrait of a time and place in modern cinema — a four-hour film that feels like a memory of your own youth.

editorial.hook: A severed ear in a field, a small town with perfect lawns, and what's under them.
editorial.synopsis: A college boy home to visit his father in hospital finds a severed human ear in a field and, because he is curious and because he is Jeffrey Beaumont, takes it to the police and then starts investigating on his own. The trail leads to a nightclub singer's apartment, a closet he hides in, and a man named Frank who inhales gas from a mask and is the most frightening person ever to appear on a screen. Lynch films the town as a 1950s postcard — roses, picket fences, a fireman waving in slow motion — and then takes the camera down into the grass where the insects are. The innocence is real and the horror is real, and the film insists they're the same place.
editorial.whyItMatters: Cahiers' top ten in 1987 and the film that made Lynch Lynch: the small-town surface and its underside, the mystery that is really about looking, the dream logic applied to the suburbs; everything from Twin Peaks to Mulholland Drive is already here.

editorial.hook: A woman in a chemical town where even the fog is poisoned, painted to match her mind.
editorial.synopsis: A woman recovering from a car accident — or from something the accident revealed — moves through the industrial outskirts of Ravenna: refineries belching yellow smoke, ships gliding past the end of a street, a shack by the water where her husband's friends talk about sex, a grey-green fog that swallows people whole. Antonioni's first colour film, and he painted the world for it — trees, grass, fruit sprayed grey, a single red wall, a shop she wants to open in a colour she can't decide. Monica Vitti plays her as a woman who feels too much in a place that feels nothing, and the film never says whether she is ill or simply the only one paying attention.
editorial.whyItMatters: Golden Lion 1964 and the moment colour became expressive rather than decorative in art cinema; Antonioni treated the palette as a character's nervous system, and the idea that landscape can be psychology — carried through Tarkovsky, Kieślowski, Wong Kar-wai — has this film as its source.
